entities.name: Asad ibn al-Furat
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Asad ibn al-Furat (d. 828 CE) was a pivotal figure in early 9th-century Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia), an influential jurist of the Maliki school of Islamic law and a leading theologian. His dual role as a scholar and a military commander profoundly shaped the political and religious landscape of the Aghlabid emirate and initiated a major expansion of Islamic power into the central Mediterranean. He is primarily remembered for instigating and leading the initial phase of the Arab conquest of Sicily, a strategic endeavor that transformed the island's millennia-old cultural and political trajectory and established a lasting Muslim presence. His career exemplifies the intertwined nature of religious authority and military ambition in the nascent Islamic states of the early Abbasid era.

Educated extensively in Medina and Kufa, Asad ibn al-Furat returned to Ifriqiya to become the chief qadi (judge) of Qayrawan under the Aghlabid emir Ziyadat Allah I (r. 817-838 CE). His legal opinions, particularly the *Asadiyya*, became a foundational text for the Maliki school in North Africa, though it often diverged from the more orthodox views of his contemporary, Sahnun. Despite his judicial eminence, Asad's most decisive action was convincing Emir Ziyadat Allah I to launch an invasion of Byzantine Sicily. In 827 CE, he personally led a formidable expeditionary force of approximately 10,000 foot soldiers and 700 cavalry, along with 100 ships, departing from Sousse. He successfully besieged Mazara del Vallo and Syracuse, establishing the first significant Muslim foothold on the island.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Asad ibn al-Furat's instigation and leadership of the 827 CE invasion initiated the Arab conquest of Sicily, fundamentally altering the island's political and cultural trajectory for over two centuries. His legal work also profoundly influenced Maliki jurisprudence in North Africa.
